slides.title: Machine translation
slides.content: Machine translation • Machine translation is a difficult task • Ultimate test for language understanding • In order to translate correctly, one needs to • understand the source language • understand the target language • have knowledge about the topic of the text to be translated • have knowledge about the culture, values, traditions, expectations of language users in both languages 2/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: A long history
slides.content: A long history • Warren Weaver (1949): “I have a text in front of me which is written in Russian, but I am going to pretend that it is really written in English, and that it has been coded in some strange symbols. All I need to do is strip off the code in order to retrieve the information contained in the text.” • First system demonstration by IBM in 1954 (word by word translation) • But machine translation turned out to be much more difficult than expected 3/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Political/commercial interest
slides.content: Political/commercial interest • The EU spends more than a billion euros on translation costs each year; (semi-)automation would save a lot of money • The US invested a lot in machine translation for intelligence acquisition • Google Translate is used by more than a billion people every month and supports close to 250 languages • Today, translation is built into browsers, phones, and chat assistants 4/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Statistical machine translation
slides.content: Statistical machine translation Why Bayes ? • Why don’t we model p(e | f) ? • By using p(f | e)P(e), we can divide the work • p(e) deals with correct usage of English • p(f | e) makes sure that French corresponds to English • We can train both models independently 14/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Statistical machine translation
slides.content: Statistical machine translation Analogy of a crime scene • f is a crime scene, and we are looking for a suspect e • p(e | f): ‘Who did it?’ • P(e): Who had a motive? • P(f | e): Could they have done it (crime scene investigation, alibi) ? • Someone can have a good motive but not the means – both are necessary 15/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Statistical machine translation
slides.content: Statistical machine translation p(e) – correct usage How to compute p(the,dog,was,running,across,the,green,field) ? • We compute the joint probability by decomposing into conditional probabilities • p(the) × p(dog|the) × p(was|the dog) × p(running|dog was) × p(across|was running) × p(the|running across) × p(green|across the) × p(field|the green) • … using only a limited context 17/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Statistical machine translation

slides.title: Statistical machine translation

slides.title: Neural machine translation
slides.content: Neural machine translation Recent history • Statistical machine translation represented the state of the art until 2015 • 2014: first sequence-to-sequence neural translation models (RNN-based) • 2016: Google Translate switches to neural; NMT widely adopted as the privileged method • 2017: the transformer, originally developed for machine translation, becomes the standard architecture • 2020s: massively multilingual models; translation as one of the many tasks of large language models 28/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Neural machine translation
slides.content: Neural machine translation Translation quality • Two dimensions of translation quality: • adequacy: does the translation preserve the meaning of the source? • fluency: is the output natural, grammatical target language? • Statistical MT: often adequate, less fluent (concatenation of translated phrases) • Neural MT: considerably more fluent; better handling of word order and morphology • One end-to-end model replaces a pipeline of separately trained components (alignment, phrase table, language model, reordering) • Fluent output can conceal adequacy errors (omissions, additions, invented content) 29/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Multilingual machine translation
slides.content: Multilingual machine translation • Classical setup: one model per language pair and direction • N languages →N(N −1) translation directions • EU: 24 official languages = 552 directions • For most pairs, hardly any parallel data exists (e.g. Finnish ↔Swahili) • Alternative: a single model trained on many languages at once 30/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Multilingual NMT
slides.content: Multilingual NMT • One shared encoder-decoder for many languages • Target language indicated by a special tag • <2nl> How are you? →Hoe gaat het? • <2fr> How are you? →Comment ça va? • All languages share the same parameters and subword vocabulary • Transfer between related languages, in particular towards languages with little parallel data 31/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Zero-shot translation
slides.content: Zero-shot translation • Train on Portuguese↔English and English↔Spanish • The model can translate Portuguese→Spanish without having seen Portuguese–Spanish sentence pairs Portuguese English Spanish training data training data zero-shot • The shared representation acts as a language-independent meaning space • Compare the interlingua of the Vauquois triangle: here the shared representation is learned from data rather than designed by hand 32/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: MT with large language models
slides.content: MT with large language models • For a large language model, translation is one instruction among others • Translate into Dutch, keeping the informal tone: “Hey, wanna grab lunch?” • No dedicated translation training: the ability results from multilingual pretraining and instruction tuning • Compared to dedicated MT systems: • document-level context and consistency • control over style and register through the prompt • terminology constraints, explanations, interactive post-editing 33/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Course evaluation: project
slides.content: Course evaluation: project • Model design, implementation, and evaluation for an NLP task or a (computational) linguistic research question • Two models from two different paradigms (symbolic, statistical, neural) • Evaluation of both models, and a comparative discussion of performance and interpretability • Two options: • Toxic Comment Classification (dataset provided) • Choose your own dataset (emotion, news topics, sarcasm, POS, NER, spam, another language, …) 34/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Project: requirements
slides.content: Project: requirements • Fixed train/dev/test split; the test set is used once, at the end • A simple baseline (majority class, rules) next to the two models • Both models are trained (or written) by you, on the same data, with the same metrics; choices (features, thresholds, hyperparameters) are made on the development data • Error analysis with concrete examples from your own test set • Every claim in the discussion is backed by an output in the notebook • Generative AI (coding assistants, chatbots) may be used and must be declared; you are responsible for every line of code and every claim 35/36 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
